bribeShareOfStake.citation: A bribe as a share of what the favor is worth to the person offering it. Spread 0.05 to 0.2; surveys of firms report bribes of a few percent to over ten percent of contract value (World Bank Enterprise Surveys, bribery incidence and depth).

corruptionNeedWeight.citation: Weight on the bribe's own size: its share of itself plus the official's month of living costs and cash on hand (between 0 and 1, so a larger bribe tempts more and levels off). Weighed beside the official's money pressure (corruptionPressureWeight), which carries most of the spread between people. Fitted Oct 24, 2026 on the adults of fourteen drawn towns (14 places drawn from all 56 with the label take-calibration, run seed fit1) and checked on fourteen more (run seed check2), with temperament carried by the shared chooser's trait term at each decision's own weight (traitWeightCorruptionOffer, traitWeightCorruptionTake), as the decision is played. Targets: the latent model of Pletzer, Bentvelzen, Oostrom and de Vries 2019 (Journal of Vocational Behavior 112:369-383, honesty-humility against workplace deviance, corrected rho -0.482, k = 15, N = 4,206) for the odds between the most and least honest thirds, computed at the rate the towns show, and Transparency International's Global Corruption Barometer (2019: about 6 percent of Americans paid a bribe for a public service in the past year) for the rate. At a $2,000 bribe from someone with a tie of 0.3, 6.3 percent of adults take it and the most corruptible third takes it 9.9 times as often as the most honest, against 11.6 from the latent model (check towns: 7.2 percent, 11.8 against 10.7). A $10,000 bribe raises takes to 9.8 percent and $50,000 to 11.8 (check towns 10.7 and 12.6); at the earlier weight of 5.5 without the pressure term a $10,000 bribe was taken by 95 percent. Spread 0.35 to 0.9 (measured with the other values held: the range in which both sets of towns keep the rate between 3 and 12 percent and the odds between thirds within a factor of 1.5 of the latent model's).

corruptionPressureWeight.citation: Weight on an official's money pressure when deciding to take a bribe: a month of their living costs against that month plus the cash they hold (0 with a deep cushion, 1 with nothing put by). Financial strain raises willingness to accept a bribe (Gorodnichenko and Sabirianova Peter 2007, Journal of Public Economics 91(5-6):963-991, on public-sector pay and bribery). Fitted Oct 24, 2026 on the adults of fourteen drawn towns (14 places drawn from all 56 with the label take-calibration, run seed fit1) and checked on fourteen more (run seed check2), with temperament carried by the shared chooser's trait term at each decision's own weight (traitWeightCorruptionOffer, traitWeightCorruptionTake), as the decision is played. Targets: the latent model of Pletzer, Bentvelzen, Oostrom and de Vries 2019 (Journal of Vocational Behavior 112:369-383, honesty-humility against workplace deviance, corrected rho -0.482, k = 15, N = 4,206) for the odds between the most and least honest thirds, computed at the rate the towns show, and Transparency International's Global Corruption Barometer (2019: about 6 percent of Americans paid a bribe for a public service in the past year) for the rate. Fitted with corruptionNeedWeight and corruptionTakeHonestPull; see the need weight's citation. Spread 5.4 to 5.8 (measured with the other values held: the range in which both sets of towns keep the rate between 3 and 12 percent and the odds between thirds within a factor of 1.5 of the latent model's).

corruptionTieWeight.citation: Weight on closeness between the two: a bribe passes through existing ties (Rose-Ackerman and Palifka 2016, Corruption and Government, ch. 6). Spread 0.5 to 2.

corruptionReputationWeight.citation: Weight on what the person who wants a favor has learned about the official: each bribe the official is known to have taken (the offerer's own knowledge record, with its source) raises the offer, with diminishing returns as the count grows. Briberies concentrate on officials already known to be receptive (Rose-Ackerman and Palifka 2016, Corruption and Government, ch. 6, on reputation and networks of exchange). Spread 0.5 to 2.

corruptionHonestPull.citation: The pull of not offering a bribe, against which the favor's worth (its log against a year of the offerer's living costs), the tie and what the offerer has heard of the official are weighed; the take and tell roles have their own pulls. Fitted Oct 24, 2026 on the offers play actually weighs: 16,228 asks kept by the trait audit in eleven played years of buildBenchWorld (Parkway, Missouri; Peacham, Vermont; Holualoa, Hawaii twice; Ilwaco, Washington; New Preston, Connecticut; Ora, Indiana; Arbela, Missouri; Jerry City, Ohio; New Britain, Connecticut; and the money branch's Peacham), each ask's favor, tie and reputation read from its kept case, with temperament carried by the shared chooser's trait term at traitWeightCorruptionOffer. Offers come from a town's lobbyists and bidding owners, not its adults at large, so a fit over every adult at one fixed favor would put the line where only money pressure reaches and no well-off lobbyist would ever offer. At 3 with the trait weight at 2, 6.9 percent of those asks become offers, near Transparency International's Global Corruption Barometer (2019: about 6 percent of Americans paid a bribe for a public service in the past year), and the third leaning most toward corruption offers 7.8 times as often as the third leaning least, against 11.0 from the latent model of Pletzer, Bentvelzen, Oostrom and de Vries 2019 (Journal of Vocational Behavior 112:369-383, honesty-humility against workplace deviance, corrected rho -0.482). The asks come from few pairs, each asked again and again, so a town's offers bunch: New Britain, Connecticut offered at every one of 578 asks, Parkway, Missouri at none of 4,407. Spread 2.5 to 3.1, measured on the same asks: from 2.5 to 2.9 the rate is 9.2 percent and the ratio 11.0 against 9.2; above 3.1 the most honest third never offers.

corruptionTakeHonestPull.citation: The pull of not taking a bribe an official is offered (the offer's own pull is corruptionHonestPull; the two sums have different ranges, so one value could not calibrate both). Fitted Oct 24, 2026 on the adults of fourteen drawn towns (14 places drawn from all 56 with the label take-calibration, run seed fit1) and checked on fourteen more (run seed check2), with temperament carried by the shared chooser's trait term at each decision's own weight (traitWeightCorruptionOffer, traitWeightCorruptionTake), as the decision is played. Targets: the latent model of Pletzer, Bentvelzen, Oostrom and de Vries 2019 (Journal of Vocational Behavior 112:369-383, honesty-humility against workplace deviance, corrected rho -0.482, k = 15, N = 4,206) for the odds between the most and least honest thirds, computed at the rate the towns show, and Transparency International's Global Corruption Barometer (2019: about 6 percent of Americans paid a bribe for a public service in the past year) for the rate. Fitted with corruptionNeedWeight and corruptionPressureWeight; see the need weight's citation for the rates and the odds between thirds. Spread 4.44 to 4.74 (measured with the other values held: the range in which both sets of towns keep the rate between 3 and 12 percent and the odds between thirds within a factor of 1.5 of the latent model's).

corruptionTellWeight.citation: Weight on how far the tie between the two parties soured when deciding to tell someone: a partner in a crime who falls out with the other is the classic leak (Rose-Ackerman and Palifka 2016, ch. 9, on whistleblowers and turned witnesses). Spread 2 to 8.

corruptionQuietPull.citation: The pull of keeping quiet about a crime one took part in. Spread 0.5 to 2.

daysPerMonth.citation: A month of daily living costs, rounded to 30 days.

corruptionReportWeight.citation: Weight on how far the person who learned of a bribe is from the official when deciding to take it to the press, against the pull of keeping quiet (corruptionQuietPull). Most people who learn of corruption don't report it, for fear of reprisal or doubt it will matter (Transparency International, Global Corruption Barometer, United States 2019); distance from the official makes reprisal and loyalty matter less. Spread 0.5 to 2.

bribeVoteWeight.citation: The most a taken bribe moves the official's position on the decision it bought, reached as the bribe grows against a month of their living costs (a member's whole position runs about -1 to 1). A bribe is a payment for a specific decision (Rose-Ackerman and Palifka 2016, Corruption and Government, ch. 4). Spread 0.5 to 2.

bribeBreachHoursPerDayOfCost.citation: Hours of closeness a payer loses toward an official who took a bribe and then voted the other way, for each day of the payer's own living costs that the bribe was worth. Corrupt bargains have no court to enforce them, so reneging is the usual cause of a falling-out between the parties (Lambsdorff 2002, Making Corrupt Deals: Contracting in the Shadow of the Law, Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 48(3):221-241). Spread 0.5 to 2.
